samples.text:
The table shows the percentage of people between 25 and 34 years old who had a university degree in five countries in the years 2000, 2010 and 2020.

In 2000, Canada had the highest percentage with 48%, and South Korea was second with 37%. The United Kingdom was 29% and Germany was 22%. Italy had the lowest percentage, only 10%.

In 2010 the figures increased in all countries. South Korea increase a lot to 63% and it become the highest, more than Canada which was 56%. The UK also went up to 46%, but Germany only increased a little to 26%. Italy percentage was 21%, that is double than 2000.

In 2020, all the countries continued to rise. South Korea reached to 70% and Canada was 64%. The UK had 57%, Germany had 36% and Italy had 29%, which was still the lowest.

Overall, the percentage of young adults with a degree went up in every country and South Korea had the biggest increase.
samples.why: Accurate figures but organised year by year, so comparison is mechanical · basic overview placed at the end · repetitive vocabulary (had, was) · several tense and word-form errors that do not impede meaning.

samples.text:
The table illustrates the proportion of 25- to 34-year-olds holding a university degree in South Korea, Canada, the UK, Germany and Italy at three points between 2000 and 2020.

Overall, the proportion of graduates in this age group grew steadily in all five countries. South Korea saw the most dramatic growth and replaced Canada as the leader, whereas Germany and Italy remained well behind the others throughout.

At the start of the period, Canada had the highest figure at 48%, followed by South Korea at 37%. Over the next decade, however, the Korean figure rose sharply to 63%, overtaking Canada, which reached 56%. By 2020, 70% of young South Koreans held a degree, compared with 64% of Canadians. The UK also experienced considerable growth, with its percentage almost doubling from 29% to 57%.

The two remaining countries had much lower levels of graduates. In Germany the percentage increased only slightly from 22% to 26% in the first decade, before rising more quickly to 36% in 2020. Italy began with the lowest rate of just 10%, but this figure has nearly tripled to 29% by the end of the period, although it was still the lowest of the five countries.
samples.why: Clear overview of universal growth and the change in leader · key trends highlighted with apt comparisons · logical paragraphing · good range of vocabulary · mostly accurate grammar with one tense slip.

samples.text:
The table compares the percentage of adults aged 25–34 with a university degree in five countries in 2000, 2010 and 2020.

The most striking feature is that graduate rates increased in every country over the two decades, although the scale of growth varied considerably. South Korea overtook Canada to occupy first place, while Italy and Germany consistently lagged behind.

South Korea's rise was the most remarkable. Starting at 37% in 2000, its rate surged to 63% in 2010 and reached 70% by 2020, a gain of 33 percentage points overall. Canada, which had led at the beginning of the period with 48%, recorded far steadier growth of eight points per decade, ending at 64%. The United Kingdom's figure almost doubled, climbing from 29% to 57%, so that it had drawn much closer to the two leading nations by the end.

At the lower end of the table, progress was more uneven. Germany saw only a marginal increase in the first decade, from 22% to 26%, before a more substantial rise to 36%. Italy, meanwhile, remained at the bottom throughout, yet its rate nearly tripled, from 10% to 29%, which represents the largest relative increase of any country.
samples.why: Clear, well-placed overview · skilful selection of absolute and relative changes · cohesion handled naturally · precise vocabulary (surged, lagged behind, marginal) · wide range of accurate structures.
